relationship: Many royal wives and the warning about a turned heart
rationale: Solomon is given seven hundred princesses and three hundred concubines, with foreign wives specified. The ruler's law forbids multiplying wives and a heart turning aside; the comparison joins the particular royal practice to the stated warning without inventing a different wife count.

relationship: Marriage with the nations and enticement to their gods
rationale: The Solomon notice recalls a prohibition against the nations' marriages lest hearts turn after idols. Exodus warns against taking and giving daughters amid foreign sacrifice because they lead the sons after their gods; the closely related warning is retained without claiming a verbatim citation.

relationship: A later warning explicitly invokes the king turned by foreign women
rationale: The source says foreign wives turned Solomon's heart after their gods in old age. Nehemiah's warning names Salomon king of Israel as one whom foreign women turned aside, supplying an explicit royal example while retaining the actual name forms and each passage's added details.

relationship: Same-chapter The named foreign cults recur in the prophetic indictment
rationale: The single composite unit lists Chemosh, the Ammonite idol called their king, Astarte and foreign-wife sacrifices, then contrasts Solomon with David. The later indictment repeats Astarte, Chemosh and the Ammonite offense and the David comparison; the original composite remains one unit, without replacing their king with another name.

relationship: The two divine appearances are recalled
rationale: The anger notice says the God from whom Solomon turned had appeared to him twice. The earlier narrative explicitly describes a second appearance and recalls His appearance at Gibeon, grounding the particular count without placing the second appearance at an independently supplied location.

relationship: The prior warning against following other gods
rationale: The narrator recalls a command not to follow other gods. The earlier divine warning to Solomon and his children names turning away, failing the commandments and serving other gods; the comparison retains that stated scope rather than claiming identical speech wording.

relationship: Same-chapter The kingdom-tearing announcement and the promise addressed to Jeroboam
rationale: The Lord announces that the kingdom will be torn from Solomon and given to his servant. Ahijah's speech to Jeroboam repeats the tearing and grants ten scepters; the surrounding introduction identifies Jeroboam as Solomon's servant, linking the announced recipient without an invented unnamed ruler.

relationship: Same-chapter The removal is deferred to the son's hand
rationale: The first declaration defers the act beyond Solomon's days for David's sake and names his son's hand. Ahijah's speech likewise says the kingdom will be taken from the son's hand and ten scepters given to Jeroboam, preserving the specified generation.

relationship: Same-chapter The David-and-Jerusalem reservation with differing scepter counts
rationale: Both statements reserve a share for Solomon's son because of David and the chosen Jerusalem. The first says one scepter, whereas the later statement says two and adds the continuing place for David and God's name; these supplied counts are reported without a numerical harmonization.

relationship: Same-chapter Ader's named hostility within the adversary account
rationale: The introduction names both Ader the Idumean and Esrom with the Damascus band account. The later summary singles out Ader's harm, resentment and rule in Edom; the link follows that named adversary without collapsing the two men's details into one biography.

relationship: Same-chapter The Edomite destruction notice receives its duration
rationale: The account of David destroying Edom and Joab going to bury those struck down includes the killing of every male. The next unit specifies Joab and Israel's six-month stay and repeats the comprehensive male-destruction wording, supplying its stated duration without adding a battle total.

relationship: Same-chapter The comprehensive destruction wording and the recorded escape
rationale: The six-month account speaks of destroying every male from Idumea. The following escape account names the boy Ader and accompanying Idumean men entering Egypt; the comparison preserves both actual descriptions without reconstructing dates or qualifying the word every.

relationship: Same-chapter The Egyptian flight and the later request to return
rationale: Ader enters Egypt as a little boy with his father's attendants. The later notice has Ader in Egypt hear of David's and Joab's deaths and request return to his land, connecting his named place of refuge with the stated return request.

relationship: Same-chapter Pharaoh's provision and subsequent marriage gift to Ader
rationale: Pharaoh supplies Ader a house and assigned bread after his journey to Egypt. The following favor notice adds the particular wife-gift, developing the same patronage relationship through distinct stated provisions rather than identifying an unrecorded Pharaoh.

relationship: Royal wife-gifts involving Thekemina's older sister
rationale: Pharaoh gives Ader a wife described as his wife's sister and Thekemina's older sister. The expanded Jeroboam account names Ano as Shishak's gift and Thekemina's older sister; the unusually specific marriage relation is compared while the clients and wife identifications remain as supplied, without certifying one marriage or ruler identity.

relationship: Distinct children in the Egyptian royal-marriage notices
rationale: Thekemina's sister bears Ader Genubath, whom Thekemina raises among Pharaoh's sons. The expanded wife-gift notice has Ano bear Jeroboam Abijah; the parallel family notices retain different fathers and sons, with Genubath's upbringing kept as its own notice instead of joining the two households.

relationship: David's reported death and the earlier death notice
rationale: Ader hears in Egypt that David has slept with his fathers. The earlier narrative records David lying down with his fathers and burial in the City of David, corroborating that specific death report without dating the Egyptian audience independently.

relationship: Joab's reported death and the earlier killing notice
rationale: The same return-request setting includes Ader hearing that Joab is dead. The earlier narrative explicitly has Benaiah put Joab to death and bury him, providing the recorded death behind that part of the report while keeping its actual agent and location.

relationship: The send-me-away requests and departures from Egypt
rationale: Ader insists that Pharaoh send him away and returns to his land. Jeroboam likewise asks Shishak to send him away and leaves for Sarira in Ephraim; the repeated request-and-departure pattern retains the different named men, royal designations and destinations.

relationship: Same-chapter Ader's Edomite rule and his adversary introduction
rationale: The harm summary names Ader as resentful and ruling in Edom. His introduction identifies him as a royal-line Idumean adversary raised against Solomon and separately includes Esrom; the comparison follows Ader without transferring Esrom's Damascus details to him.

relationship: Jeroboam's Ephraimite-servant introductions with maternal details preserved
rationale: Both introduce Jeroboam from Ephraim's region as Solomon's servant. The first calls him Nebat's son and a widow's son, while the expanded introduction names his mother Sarira and calls her a prostitute; those supplied descriptions remain intact without an invented family history.

relationship: Citadel and David-city enclosure language in the revolt notices
rationale: The explanation of raising hands against Solomon names the citadel and closure of the City of David. The expanded notice also connects Jeroboam's rise with the citadel, city enclosure and Ephraim's burdens; the first unit's builder pronoun is not expanded into an independently resolved personal attribution.

relationship: Solomon's appointment over Joseph's burdens
rationale: Solomon sees Jeroboam's ability and work and appoints him over the burdens of Joseph's house. The expanded introduction likewise states Solomon's appointment over Joseph's burdens and calls him ruler of the staff, retaining the particular appointment rather than a generic labor connection.

relationship: Garment-sign settings with different named prophets
rationale: Ahijah the Shilonite meets Jeroboam on the road wearing a new garment. The expanded Shechem notice gives a new-garment command to Shemaiah the Elamite and a twelve-piece sign; the shared sign setting is compared without substituting either prophet's name or asserting identical chronology.

relationship: Same-chapter The twelve torn pieces are interpreted by the ten-piece command
rationale: Ahijah tears his own new garment into twelve pieces. His next speech tells Jeroboam to take ten and explains the kingdom-tearing gift of ten scepters, supplying the stated interpretation of that particular action.

relationship: Ahijah's word is expressly invoked in the narrator's explanation
rationale: Ahijah promises Jeroboam ten scepters through the kingdom-tearing word. The later narrator says the turn of events establishes the Lord's word through Ahijah the Shilonite concerning Jeroboam, giving an explicit narrative reference to that prophecy rather than an independently inferred date.

relationship: The reserved share and the named continuing supporters of David's house
rationale: The prophecy reserves two scepters for the David-and-Jerusalem reason. The later kingship notice names Judah's scepter and Benjamin as those remaining with David's house, allowing the stated remnant descriptions to be compared without an unrecorded tribe-count reconciliation.

relationship: Same-chapter The prophetic cult indictment recalls the composite apostasy account
rationale: The accusation names Astarte, Chemosh, Moab's idols and the Ammonite offense, then says he did not follow David's way. The earlier composite narrates those particular cult provisions and the same David contrast, retaining its single supplied reference and actual idol descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter The David-related qualification retains the actual opposition clause
rationale: Both qualify kingdom removal for David's sake. The earlier statement defers the act beyond Solomon's days; this one says the whole kingdom will not be taken from his hand and also says God will oppose him through his life, preserving that clause instead of describing unqualified protection.

relationship: Same-chapter The ten-scepter gift with the removal generation specified
rationale: The later statement takes the kingdom from the son's hand and gives Jeroboam ten scepters. The earlier ten-piece explanation speaks of tearing from Solomon's hand; the comparison retains the repeated ten-scepter gift and the stated generational distinction.

relationship: Same-chapter The chosen-city reservation retains two versus one
rationale: The later reservation gives the son two scepters for David's continuing place in chosen Jerusalem. The first reservation says one scepter for David and Jerusalem; the shared reasons and the differing actual numbers are both retained rather than silently made equal.

relationship: Promised kingship over Israel and the narrated royal appointment
rationale: The promise tells Jeroboam that he will be king over Israel. The later assembly calls him and makes him king over Israel after hearing of his return from Egypt, providing the express political appointment corresponding to that named promise.

relationship: The faithful-house promise explicitly appeals to the Davidic house
rationale: Jeroboam is conditionally promised a faithful house as God built for David. The Samuel promise names David's seed, house, kingdom and throne and describes correction without withdrawal of mercy; the comparison preserves the different conditions and scopes rather than making the promises identical.

relationship: The two accounts of Jeroboam's flight to Shishak
rationale: Both say Solomon sought Jeroboam's death and that he fled to Shishak king of Egypt until Solomon died. The expanded notice adds fear, while both retain the same named refugee, king and end point without an added travel timetable.

relationship: Regnal closing formulas point to differently named records
rationale: Solomon's closing notice refers his remaining acts and discernment to the Book of Solomon's Acts. Rehoboam's notice likewise directs remaining acts to the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah; the literary formula is compared without claiming the two titles are one work or that either work has been independently read.

relationship: The forty-year Solomon reign notices
rationale: Kings gives Solomon's reign in Jerusalem as forty years. Chronicles likewise gives forty years over all Israel; the common ruler and duration are retained while each notice's geographic scope remains its own.

relationship: Solomon's death, David-city burial and Rehoboam's succession
rationale: Both notices have Solomon fall asleep, burial in David's city and succession by Rehoboam his son. Kings additionally places Jeroboam's Egyptian return within its longer closing unit; that extra material is not imported into the shorter Chronicles notice.

relationship: Same-chapter Shechem's repeated royal-gathering setting
rationale: The first notice has all Israel come to Shechem to make Rehoboam king. The expanded account again places Rehoboam and the gathered tribes at Shechem, but also includes Jeroboam's gathering and a named prophetic sign; the particular shared setting is retained without merging every detail.

relationship: Same-chapter The people's address introduces its particular grievance
rationale: The people begin their speech to Rehoboam. The next supplied unit gives the actual demand to lighten his father's heavy collar and harsh servitude, identifying the content of that address without inventing the absent 12:2.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated heavy-collar petition with different added details
rationale: Both petitions ask that the father's heavy collar be lightened and promise service. The expanded wording adds the burden of the royal table, while the first names harsh servitude; these particular demands are compared without adding the table clause to the first speech.

relationship: Same-chapter The three-day instruction is expressly recalled when Israel returns
rationale: Rehoboam tells the people to return after three days. The later notice says Israel comes on the third day as he had instructed, explicitly connecting the appointment with the reported return.

relationship: Same-chapter The elders' requested advice supplies the servant-and-good-words answer
rationale: The king asks the elders who had stood before Solomon how to answer the people. Their response advises serving the people and speaking good words, specifying the counsel sought in that exact exchange.

relationship: Same-chapter The good-words counsel contrasts with the delivered threats
rationale: The elders advise service and good words leading to lasting service from the people. Rehoboam's actual reply instead adds to the collar and threatens scorpions, contrasting the particular proposed approach with the recorded answer.

relationship: Same-chapter Rejecting elder counsel and seeking the companions' response
rationale: The first account says Rehoboam abandons the elders' advice and consults the young men brought up with him. The expanded account also dismisses that counsel and summons his companions, then supplies their boast and scorpion threat; the parallel consultation sequence retains each account's wording.

relationship: Same-chapter The young men's requested answer supplies their actual proposed speech
rationale: Rehoboam repeats the people's lightened-collar request and asks the young men what to answer. Their next speech answers with the little-part boast, heavier collar and scorpions, identifying the concrete counsel behind his choice.

relationship: Same-chapter The instructed harsh speech and the delivered answer
rationale: The young men frame an answer to the father's heavy-collar complaint and add the little-part boast. The reported answer follows their counsel with a heavier collar and scorpion threat; the comparison does not insert the boast itself into the shorter delivered speech.

relationship: Same-chapter The heavier-collar and scorpion threats are actually delivered
rationale: The advised speech contrasts the father's whips with scorpions and promises an added collar. Rehoboam's reply repeats those specific threats, providing the narrative execution of the young men's advice.

relationship: Same-chapter The returned assembly keeps the specified appointment
rationale: Israel returns on the third day and the narrator quotes the earlier instruction. The original three-day dismissal supplies that appointment, allowing the precise repeated interval to be checked.

relationship: Same-chapter The harsh answer departs from the elders' good-words advice
rationale: The king answers harshly and abandons the elders' counsel. Their actual advice was to serve the people and speak good words, grounding the narrator's contrast in the particular advice rather than a generic preference for age.

relationship: Same-chapter The final reply repeats the selected threats
rationale: The delivered answer adds to the father's collar and contrasts whips with scorpions. Those same particular contrasts were the young men's proposed speech, making the retained relationship one of counsel and execution.

relationship: The narrator points back to Ahijah's kingdom-tearing word
rationale: The narrator attributes the turn to the Lord establishing Ahijah's word concerning Jeroboam. Ahijah's speech to Jeroboam promises the torn kingdom's ten scepters, supplying the particular earlier royal word behind that reference.

relationship: The no-share-in-David and tents proclamation recurs
rationale: Israel's response denies a share in David and inheritance in Jesse's son and calls the people to their tents. Sheba's horn proclamation uses those same distinctive expressions in another departure from David, without equating the two rebellions or their leaders.

relationship: Same-chapter Rehoboam's Jerusalem departure and the expanded chariot notice
rationale: After Adoniram's stoning, Rehoboam escapes to Jerusalem. The expanded account describes dispersal from Shechem and his chariot departure to Jerusalem, retaining that common movement while not inserting Adoniram's death into the shorter expanded notice.

relationship: Same-chapter Rejection of David's house follows the explicit no-share declaration
rationale: The narrator summarizes Israel's rejection of David's house. The preceding public declaration denies a share in David and inheritance in Jesse's son, providing the particular speech behind that summary rather than a claim about every later date.

relationship: Jeroboam's appointment corresponds to the named royal promise
rationale: The assembly makes Jeroboam king over Israel and names the Davidic supporters separately. The earlier promise explicitly says Jeroboam will be king over Israel, grounding the royal comparison without extending the promise to unreported tribal arrangements.

relationship: Same-chapter Judah-and-Benjamin mobilization with distinct figures and timing
rationale: The first muster names a hundred twenty thousand young warriors of Judah and Benjamin to restore Rehoboam's kingdom. The expanded notice gives a beginning-of-year expedition against Jeroboam at Shechem without that number; the common mobilization and the actual differences remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter The word to Shemaiah introduces the prohibition of brother-war
rationale: The Lord's word comes to Shemaiah the man of God. The speech it introduces forbids fighting their Israelite brothers and orders return because the matter is from God, identifying the actual message rather than inventing another prophecy.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated named recipients of the anti-war message
rationale: The first address names Rehoboam, Judah's house, Benjamin and the rest of the people. The expanded Shemaiah message repeats that recipient group and the instruction not to fight, connecting the stated addressees with the repeated message.

relationship: Same-chapter The prohibition and reported obedience recur in the expanded account
rationale: Both accounts prohibit fighting Israelite brothers because the matter comes from the Lord and order return home. Both then report listening and refraining from going, retaining the actual command-and-response wording across the two supplied sections.

relationship: Rehoboam's regnal notices preserve differing ages, reigns and maternal forms
rationale: The expanded notice gives Rehoboam sixteen at accession and twelve years in Jerusalem, with Naanan daughter of Anan named as mother. The later regnal notice gives forty-one and seventeen years and Naamah the Ammonite. The common Rehoboam-son-of-Solomon and Jerusalem framework is compared without reconciling those figures or maternal identities.

relationship: The repeated appointment over Joseph's burdens
rationale: The expanded introduction says Solomon made Jeroboam ruler of the staff over the burdens of Joseph's house. The earlier notice also records Solomon appointing the able young worker over that named house's burdens; the particular appointment is shared while the expanded building and chariot details remain additional.

relationship: The repeated flight from Solomon to Shishak
rationale: Both accounts say Solomon seeks Jeroboam's death, he flees to Shishak king of Egypt and remains until Solomon dies. The expanded account's fear is kept as its own addition, without constructing a separate travel chronology.

relationship: Egyptian return requests after news of a king's death
rationale: Jeroboam hears Solomon is dead and asks Shishak to send him to his land. Ader's earlier Egyptian audience follows news of David's and Joab's deaths and includes a similar send-me-away request; the specific narrative pattern leaves the clients, deceased rulers and hosts distinct.

relationship: Thekemina-sister marriage gifts with different husbands and sons
rationale: Shishak gives Jeroboam Ano, Thekemina's older sister, who bears Abijah. The Ader account likewise gives a Thekemina-sister wife and names her son Genubath, with a separate upbringing notice; the repeated family pattern does not certify identical marriages or children.

relationship: Jeroboam's Egyptian return to Sarira is also in Solomon's closing notice
rationale: The expanded account has Jeroboam leave Egypt and come to Sarira in Ephraim, then describes the gathering and stockade. Solomon's longer death notice also has Jeroboam hear in Egypt and return to Sarira in Ephraim, matching the named destination without imposing a reconstructed date.

relationship: Same-chapter The child's illness inquiry and its later death oracle and report
rationale: Jeroboam's child becomes very ill and he sends Ano to inquire whether the child will live. Ahijah later predicts the death notice and the narrative reports the child's death as the woman enters Sarira, connecting that particular inquiry with its stated outcome without creating absent chapter-14 illness verses.

relationship: The Shiloh prophet named Ahijah appears in both settings
rationale: The expanded account introduces Ahijah at Shiloh with the Lord's word and gives his age as sixty. The road account calls the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite; the shared name and Shiloh designation are retained without importing that supplied age or the wife's visit into the road scene.

relationship: Same-chapter The prescribed food-gift list is carried with specific added detail
rationale: The woman takes loaves, two little cakes, grapes and honey. The preceding instruction lists those kinds of gifts for the man of God and mentions cakes for his children; the link follows the actual preparations while preserving the later number two and the prophet's dim-sight notice.

relationship: Same-chapter Ano's arrival carries out the named illness inquiry
rationale: Ahijah tells his attendant to meet Ano, Jeroboam's wife, and announces harsh things. Jeroboam's earlier instruction sends that named wife to inquire about the sick child, identifying the mission of her arrival without adding a disguise or a changed name.

relationship: Same-chapter The predicted Sarira death greeting and the actual return
rationale: Ahijah predicts that upon entering Sarira the woman's young women will meet her with news that the child is dead. The return report has the child die as she enters Sarira and an outcry meet her, preserving both the specific prediction and the shorter outcome wording.

relationship: The Jeroboam-house destruction oracle and the closing sin judgment
rationale: The expanded oracle threatens destruction of Jeroboam's male household and gives particular city-dog and field-bird fates. The later closing judgment calls his priestly practice a sin bringing destruction and disappearance to his house; the shared named-house doom does not add the oracle's animal details to that later statement.

relationship: Same-chapter The actual return follows the child's death prediction
rationale: The woman enters Sarira, the child dies and the outcry comes to meet her. The prior oracle had named Sarira's gate and a death greeting from the young women; the link reports correspondence without making every shorter outcome clause a repeated quotation.

relationship: The garment division parallels Ahijah's sign while keeping Shemaiah named
rationale: Shemaiah the Elamite receives a new-garment command, twelve-piece division and ten-piece gift to Jeroboam in the Shechem setting. Ahijah the Shilonite performs a new-garment division and ten-piece interpretation on the road; the particular sign is compared without equating the differently named prophets or their narrated settings.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated petition and three-day answer appointment
rationale: The expanded petition asks relief from the father's collar and table burden and receives a three-day answer appointment. The first exchange also requests collar relief and promises service, followed by a three-day dismissal, retaining the added table detail as supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter The elder consultation is requested in both versions
rationale: Rehoboam calls for elders to consult about answering the people on the third day. The earlier consultation likewise asks the elders how to answer; the expanded unit's reported response is retained as written rather than being silently replaced by the earlier good-words counsel.

relationship: Same-chapter The companions' boast and scorpions repeat with distinct wording
rationale: The expanded companions advise the little-part and father's-loins boast and contrast whips with ruling by scorpions. The earlier young-men counsel includes the same boast and scorpion contrast but also adds the collar and uses discipline wording, preserving those actual speech differences.

relationship: Same-chapter Accepted companion counsel and the earlier recorded answer
rationale: The expanded notice says the saying pleased Rehoboam and he answered as the young men advised. The earlier account records the harsh answer and the collar-and-scorpion words, connecting the stated acceptance with that fuller advice-and-answer account without adding its full speech to this shorter unit.

relationship: Same-chapter The no-share and tents acclamation repeats
rationale: Both public cries deny a share in David or inheritance in Jesse's son and direct Israel to its tents. The expanded cry adds that the man is unfit for ruler or leader, while the earlier speech tells David to shepherd his own house, retaining the distinct final clauses.

relationship: Same-chapter Dispersal, Jerusalem flight and the continuing Judah-Benjamin following
rationale: The expanded notice has people disperse from Shechem, Rehoboam leave by chariot for Jerusalem and Judah and Benjamin follow him. The earlier account also gives Jerusalem flight and the two continuing supporters, while separately narrating Adoniram's death; that extra event is not inserted into the expanded departure.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated Judah-and-Benjamin war muster
rationale: The expanded expedition gathers Judah and Benjamin at the year's beginning to fight Jeroboam at Shechem. The first muster names those same groups, a hundred twenty thousand and the restoration purpose; the comparison keeps the differing timing, destination and number statements.

relationship: Same-chapter The Shemaiah message repeats the named audience and prohibition
rationale: The expanded Lord's word through Shemaiah names Rehoboam, Judah, Benjamin and the remainder and forbids war against brothers because the matter comes from God. The first message gives the same named prophet, audience and command, without requiring an independently reconstructed single delivery date.

relationship: Same-chapter The obedience notice repeats listening and refraining
rationale: The expanded ending says they listened to the Lord's word and refrained from going. The first prohibition also ends with listening and stopping their going according to that word, preserving the concrete repeated response.

relationship: Same-chapter Shechem in the royal gathering and Jeroboam's residence
rationale: The royal-gathering notice places Rehoboam at Shechem for Israel to make him king. This building notice has Jeroboam build and reside in Shechem in Ephraim before building Penuel, comparing the city's distinct royal settings without identifying a modern site or dating the construction relative to the gathering.

relationship: Same-chapter The fear of a restored Davidic kingdom is explained
rationale: Jeroboam's inward concern is that the kingdom will return to David's house. His next reasoning specifies Jerusalem sacrifice, the people's returning hearts and his feared death, supplying the stated grounds rather than treating the fear as a verified prediction.

relationship: Same-chapter Fear of Jerusalem worship is followed by the heifer policy
rationale: Jeroboam fears the Jerusalem sacrifices will turn the people's hearts to the Lord and their lord Rehoboam and lead to his death. His following policy says their Jerusalem journeys should be enough and introduces the two golden heifers, linking the stated motive with his particular alternative.

relationship: Golden bovine images and the Egypt-deliverance proclamation
rationale: Jeroboam's two golden heifers are introduced as Israel's gods who brought them up from Egypt. Aaron's cast calf is proclaimed with closely matching deliverance words and an altar and feast, preserving two heifers versus one calf rather than merging the episodes.

relationship: Bethel's named cult placement and the later altar confrontation
rationale: Jeroboam puts one heifer in Bethel and another in Dan. The next chapter specifically places him at Bethel's altar when the Judah man of God arrives; the connection follows the named Bethel setting without moving the Dan image into that scene.

relationship: Same-chapter The sin verdict refers back to the heifer policy
rationale: The narrator calls this matter a sin and says the people went before the one as far as Dan. The preceding policy supplies the two heifers and their Egypt-deliverance proclamation, identifying the narrated worship arrangement without inventing a different route or image count.

relationship: The later appointment notice repeats and expands the priestly practice
rationale: Jeroboam appoints priests from some of the people who are not sons of Levi. The later notice says he again appointed priests from some people and consecrated whoever wished, retaining the first lineage statement and the later willingness criterion as their distinct details.

relationship: The fifteenth-day feast retains eighth versus seventh month
rationale: Jeroboam's feast is on the fifteenth of the eighth month and is described as like Judah's feast. Leviticus assigns the Feast of Tents to the fifteenth of the seventh month for seven days; the particular date comparison preserves the month difference without certifying identical observance.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated date and the heart-fashioned feast
rationale: The final notice repeats the fifteenth of the eighth month and going up to the made altar, adding that the feast was fashioned from his heart. The preceding account names Bethel and comparison with Judah's feast, grounding the particular altar-and-date repetition while retaining the differing descriptions.

relationship: The altar-offering scene continues into the prophetic arrival
rationale: Jeroboam is standing at the altar to offer sacrifice when the Judah man of God arrives. The preceding chapter closes with Jeroboam going up to the altar at his fashioned feast to offer sacrifice, supplying the particular narrated cult setting rather than an invented interval.

relationship: The named Josiah and human-bones announcement is expressly recalled
rationale: The oracle names Josiah and burning human bones upon the altar. The later account names Josiah taking bones from tombs and burning them on the altar according to the man of God's word while Jeroboam stood there, giving an explicit narrative reference without replacing any named ruler.

relationship: Same-chapter The split-altar and poured-fat portent receives its stated outcome
rationale: The man of God gives a portent that the altar will split and its fat pour out. The following notice reports those same two events according to the portent by the Lord's word, directly connecting prediction with its narrated occurrence.

relationship: Same-chapter The withered hand is the subject of the restoration petition
rationale: Jeroboam's extended hand withers and cannot be drawn back after his seizure command. He then asks the man of God to entreat the Lord for restoration, followed by the restored-hand notice; the comparison stays with the particular hand and does not assign an unstated medical diagnosis.

relationship: Same-chapter The narrated altar sign repeats the earlier portent
rationale: The split altar and pouring fat are reported according to the man of God's portent. His earlier announcement names exactly those two events, providing the stated word behind the narrative's own correspondence claim.

relationship: Same-chapter The restored hand contrasts with its earlier condition
rationale: The king asks for the Lord's favor and the text reports his hand restored as before. The earlier condition is the hand withered after stretching it against the man of God; the link does not resolve the restoration sentence's pronoun into an additional independently assigned agent.

relationship: Same-chapter The meal-and-gift invitation meets the refusal
rationale: The king invites the man of God to his house for a meal and a gift. The reply refuses entrance and bread or water even for half the house, answering that particular invitation rather than asserting the Lord prohibited every possible gift.

relationship: Same-chapter The refusal is explained by the reported command
rationale: The refusal names bread and water in that place. The following explanation reports the Lord's prohibition of those acts and the return road, grounding the food refusal while leaving the road clause as an additional actual command.

relationship: Same-chapter The original food-and-road command is repeated to another host
rationale: The man of God first reports the prohibition of bread, water and return by the same road. He later repeats those three restrictions in answering the old prophet's invitation, preserving the concrete command rather than a general rule about all hospitality.

relationship: Same-chapter The alternate return road follows the reported route command
rationale: He takes another road rather than the one by which he came to Bethel. The preceding reported Lord's command forbids return by the traveled road, matching the particular route action without claiming his later food conduct also remained obedient.

relationship: Same-chapter The sons' report prompts the specific road inquiry
rationale: The old prophet's sons report the man of God's Bethel deeds and words. Their father's next question asks which road he took, and the sons show it, connecting the actual report with the information sought for the pursuit.

relationship: Same-chapter The road information leads to the identification encounter
rationale: The sons show the road taken by the Judah man of God. The subsequent pursuit finds him and asks whether he is that Judah visitor, linking the stated information with the particular identifying question without identifying an unrecorded route.

relationship: Same-chapter The saddled donkey is used for the described pursuit
rationale: The old prophet asks his sons to saddle the donkey and mounts it. The next unit reports his pursuit and finding the man under an oak, giving the specified transport's purpose without connecting the oak to an unrelated tree episode.

relationship: Same-chapter The encountered man is identified against the sons' earlier report
rationale: The pursuer asks whether the seated man is the man of God from Judah and receives I am. His sons had reported the Bethel deeds and words to their father, providing the narrated report behind this identification rather than an independently recovered personal name.

relationship: Same-chapter Two different hosts invite the man of God to eat
rationale: The old prophet invites him to come and eat bread. The king had earlier invited him to his house for a meal with a gift, repeating a meal invitation under the stated food restriction with different speakers and without assigning either host an unreported testing motive or adding the royal gift to the second invitation.

relationship: Same-chapter The food-and-water refusal repeats
rationale: The man refuses to return with the old prophet or eat bread and drink water there. His earlier royal reply also refuses bread and water in the place, retaining the same dietary response while the half-house offer belongs only to that earlier exchange.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated quotation keeps the route restriction as well as food
rationale: The answer to the old prophet quotes the Lord's bread, water and traveled-road restrictions. The earlier explanation to the king reports the same three actual prohibitions, supporting a precise repeated-command link.

relationship: Same-chapter The claimed angelic permission conflicts with the later judgment
